children: By Staff Writer

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has accredited Ugandan biotechnology and pharmaceutical manufacturer, Dei BioPharma Ltd, to the African Pooled Procurement Mechanism (APPM).

This gives the Ugandan company a pass into the continental medicines market as the African Union and African governments seek to aggregate their purchasing power, strengthen supply security, and create more predictable markets for manufacturers on the continent.

In an August 28 notification, Dr Mariatou Tala Jallow, director of the APPM at Africa CDC, said Dei BioPharma had met the technical requirements for participation as a supplier under the pooled procurement arrangement.

The AU and Africa CDC have set a target of meeting at least 60 percent of Africa’s health-product needs through African manufacturing by 2040. However, achieving that ambition is heavily dependent on creating viable product pipelines, regulatory capacity, quality systems, investment, skilled human capital and markets capable of sustaining manufacturers.

The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the vulnerability created by Africa’s dependence on external sources for medicines, vaccines and other health technologies. Supply disruptions, foreign-exchange pressures and competition for scarce products reinforced the case for developing local and regional manufacturing capacity.

For Uganda, the registration provides a link between its emerging domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity and a continental procurement system designed to address highly fragmented health-product markets, one of Africa’s longstanding weaknesses.

Dei BioPharma’s registration comes at a significant stage in the company’s development as it seeks to move beyond establishing manufacturing infrastructure towards building a portfolio of regulated products for markets beyond Uganda.

According to founder and medical innovator Dr Matthias Magoola, the company has submitted 65 product applications to Uganda’s National Drug Authority (NDA), with 40 approved for manufacture and 14 approved for sale.
Two products illustrate the type of health challenges that African manufacturers could increasingly address.
HYXUREA, a hydroxyurea 500mg tablet, is aimed at improving access to treatment for sickle-cell disease, which carries a particularly heavy burden in sub-Saharan Africa.

The World Health Organization estimates that 7.74 million people globally were living with sickle-cell disease in 2021, with nearly 80 percent of the global burden occurring in sub-Saharan Africa. WHO estimates that about 240,000 children are born with the condition in Africa each year. Yet, access to essential medicines remains uneven.

WHO Africa has previously reported that hydroxyurea was available in only 11 countries in the region, highlighting the gap between disease burden and access to treatment. A similar challenge exists with TRENMIC, Dei BioPharma’s tranexamic acid 500 mg tablet, used in the management of serious bleeding.
The issue has direct implications for maternal health.
In 2023, about 260,000 women died from pregnancy- and childbirth-related causes globally, with sub-Saharan Africa accounting for approximately 182,000 deaths, or 70 percent of the total.

Obstetric haemorrhage remains a major contributor to maternal mortality, particularly where access to essential medicines, skilled personnel and emergency care is limited.“The significance of products such as these is therefore less about individual commercial brands and more about the capacity to ensure that quality-assured medicines relevant to Africa’s major health challenges are available through reliable supply systems,” Magoola says.
He argues that Africa’s pharmaceutical needs extend well beyond conventional medicines to include vaccines, diagnostics, oncology products, hormones, biological products and biosimilars.
Dei BioPharma’s ambitions similarly encompass conventional medicines, injectables, oncology products, biological products, biosimilars, diagnostics and vaccines.

The broader objective, Magoola says, is to build technological capacity that can support Africa’s health security rather than relying primarily on imported finished products. Africa needs an ecosystem connecting scientific innovation, product development, regulation, quality manufacturing, financing, procurement and predictable markets, he adds.

According to several analyses, African pharmaceutical companies have historically struggled with fragmented national procurement systems, which can impede efforts to achieve the scale and demand predictability needed to justify investment in manufacturing and product development.
The APPM seeks to address that constraint by aggregating demand across participating countries. So far, the Africa CDC has registered 574 health product manufacturers.

The potential of pooled procurement to reduce prices of essential medicines was demonstrated when Africa CDC’s first APPM tender for essential reproductive, maternal and newborn health medicines achieved prices that were 30 -90 percent below participating member state benchmarks.
Beyond price reductions, larger and more predictable markets are seen as an incentive for manufacturers to invest in regulatory approvals, technology, production capacity and new products.

While participation in APPM gives the Ugandan manufacturer a platform from which eligible products can potentially compete for aggregated African demand as its portfolio expands, individual products will still have to satisfy applicable regulatory, technical, quality and procurement requirements.
